title: The Progressives
objective: After this level you can explain how muckrakers and reformers took on monopolies, unsafe food and corrupt city machines.
summary: Ida Tarbell exposed Standard Oil, broken up in 1911. The Jungle (1906) led to the Meat Inspection and Pure Food and Drug Acts. Nast’s cartoons helped topple Boss Tweed; Jane Addams founded Hull-House.

cards.headline: A novel about a Chicago meatpacking plant made Congress act.
cards.body: The Progressives believed that if people saw what was happening, they would demand change. Reporters, cartoonists and reformers set out to show them.

cards.headline: The reporter and the monopoly
cards.body: Remember Standard Oil? Ida Tarbell’s History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), first serialized in McClure’s magazine, exposed its unfair tactics and railroad rebates. In 1911 the Supreme Court ruled that Standard Oil had broken the Sherman Antitrust Act and ordered it split into 34 companies. From book to breakup took just seven years.

cards.headline: The Jungle
cards.body: Upton Sinclair’s novel The Jungle (1906) exposed filthy, dangerous conditions in Chicago’s meatpacking plants. Readers were disgusted, and public outrage helped pass the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act, both in 1906.
cards.callout: The Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act both passed in 1906

cards.headline: Cleaning up the cities
cards.body: Boss William Tweed’s Tammany Hall ring plundered New York City of an estimated $30 million to $200 million. Thomas Nast’s cartoons helped expose it, and Tweed was convicted in 1873. Reformers also built. In 1889 Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull-House in Chicago, offering immigrant neighbors classes, childcare and job help.

cards.headline: The Progressives: explained
learned: Tarbell’s reporting led to Standard Oil’s 1911 breakup
The Jungle led to the 1906 food and meat laws
Nast’s cartoons helped topple Boss Tweed

questions.prompt: Match each reformer with their work.

pairs.right: History of the Standard Oil Company

questions.explanation: Ida Tarbell wrote the History of the Standard Oil Company, Upton Sinclair wrote The Jungle, Thomas Nast drew the cartoons that exposed Boss Tweed, and Jane Addams co-founded Hull-House.

questions.prompt: How did Ida Tarbell help bring down Standard Oil’s monopoly?

options.label: She bought a controlling share of the company’s stock and broke it up
options.rationale: She was a reporter, not an investor.

options.label: She wrote the Sherman Antitrust Act and got it passed
options.rationale: Her reporting exposed the company; she didn’t write the law.

options.label: Her reporting exposed its tactics; in 1911 the Court split it up
She organized a strike of the company’s oil workers
options.rationale: She was a reporter, and her weapon was her writing.

questions.explanation: Tarbell exposed Standard Oil’s tactics and rebates; in 1911 the Court ruled it broke antitrust law and split it into 34 companies.

questions.prompt: The Jungle exposed Chicago’s meatpacking plants. How did cattle and pigs first reach the Americas?

options.label: They were native to the Great Plains all along
Across the Atlantic, in the Columbian Exchange after 1492
The first Americans brought them over Beringia
options.rationale: The first Americans had not domesticated them.

options.label: Chicago breeders created them from wild bison in the 1800s

questions.explanation: Cattle and pigs came to the Americas in the Columbian Exchange that followed 1492.
